newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel approves housing for Jews in East Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Israel approves housing for Jews in East Jerusalem.

text.p: Israel on Tuesday gave penultimate approval to build 132 homes for Jews in the heart of an Arab neighbourhood in East Jerusalem in a move that angered Palestinians and leftist Israelis.

Israel's Jerusalem municipal planning commission approved the plan for Jewish housing at the Ras al-Amoud neighbourhood, where about 11,000 Palestinians live. It now needs ministerial approval to go ahead.
"It is good news on the festival of lights (Hanukkah), it's another reason for joy," Israeli Interior Minister Eli Suissa told Reuters during a visit to a Jewish settlement near Hebron.
Faisal al-Husseini, the top PLO representative in Jerusalem, swiftly slammed the decision calling it a "time bomb" and warned it will ignite a new outburst of violence if implemented.
"I am saying now that this project, if implemented, it will bring another explosion," Hussein said.
He was referring to a wave of violence in September sparked by Israel's opening an entrance to a tunnel near Moslem sites in Jerusalem. Sixty Palestinians and 15 Israelis were killed in the clashes.
"And I believe this time it will be for more time and it will be more difficult to stop it," Husseini said.

Israel has encircled Arab East Jerusalem with Jewish neighbourhoods since it captured the city along with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East War. But apart from the settling of some 3,000 Jews inside the walled Old City, it would be the first time that Israel tried to settle Jews in the heart of an Arab community.
The housing plan must be approved by Suissa, who said the process would take several months before it is ready for implementation.

Officials in Israel's former government, who refused to approve the project when it was first introduced in 1992, have warned that the plan to build Jewish housing in East Jerusalem's Ras al-Amud neighbourhood could provoke fresh violence.

The land for the project is owned by a Miami-based businessman, Dr Irving Moskowitz, who is known for his support of Jewish settlement activity in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. An Arab family now resides on the land.

The Peace Now movement, which lobbied against the plan, said the project was politically motivated and vowed to demonstrate against it. Peace Now said if Suissa gave his approval it would appeal the decision in court.

"The attempt of Dr Moskowitz, backed by the Jerusalem municipality and by the Minister of Interior Mr Eli Suissa will undoubtedly create a major political problem and a chain reaction similar to that following the opening of the 'Tunnel'," a statement faxed to Reuters by Peace Now movement said.
The status of East Jerusalem is up for negotiations in final status peace talks which have yet to resume under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who took office in June.

There are now some 160,000 Jews living in East Jerusalem and around 155,000 Palestinians. The PLO wants East Jerusalem to be the capital of a future Palestinian state. Israel regards the city as part of its "eternal" capital.
